units.translation: 4. The forms of the subjunctive and the participle ὤν [being] are the same as in all other authors, except that there are no examples of the dual. Of the infinitive εἶναι [to be], there is one example of the epic form ἔμμεν [to be] in Sophocles Ant. 623, none in Aeschylus.

5. The first person singular of the imperfect has the Attic form ἢ [I was], which I discussed in Thes. vol. 3 p. 262 and, as far as Sophocles is concerned, in Lex. Soph. p. 1415. There are two examples in Aeschylus: Ag. 1637, restored by Porson for ň, and Ch. 523 in the compound παρῆ [I was present], which Porson restored for πάρει [you are present]. Examples of the other persons are ἦσθα [you were], ἦν [he/she/it was] (the epic form ἔσκεν [he/she/it was] once, Pers. 656), and ἦμεν [we were], ἦτε [you (pl.) were], ἦσαν [they were].

6. There are no examples of the first person singular of the future ἔσομαι [I will be] in Aeschylus. The second person singular ending ἔσει [you will be] is nowhere preserved in M, which consistently offers ἔσῃ [you will be], and similarly in other verbs it often has ἢ for ei. The third person singular ἔσται [he/she/it will be] is quite frequent; but the form ἔσεται [he/she/it will be] which is read in M at Pers. 121 is a corruption of ᾄσεται [he/she/it will sing], which Burney restored. The infinitive ἔσεσθαι [to be about to be] is in the interpolated verse Pr. 835.
